title: No Favoritism, and Faith That Works
summary: James condemns the practice of honoring rich visitors and humiliating poor ones in the assembly, because God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith and favoritism breaks the royal law of love. He then argues that faith without deeds is dead: faith that says kind words to the hungry and does nothing cannot save. Abraham and Rahab were justified by what they did, showing that living faith always works.
story: Chapter 1 ended by defining true religion as care for orphans and widows and warning against hearing without doing. Chapter 2 develops both themes. First James shows what it looks like when a church fails the poor, and then he takes up the deeper question behind it: what kind of faith leaves a brother or sister hungry and cold? The chapter looks back to Abraham, the father of Israel's faith, and to Rahab, the Canaanite woman who sheltered Israel's spies before Jericho, and it looks forward to judgment, when mercy will count. It contains the most debated verses in the letter, the ones that led readers ever since to ask how James and Paul fit together.
historical:
The assembly James pictures is called in Greek a synagōgē, the same word used for a Jewish synagogue (translated “meeting” in verse 2). Early Jewish believers in Jesus could naturally call their gathering by this name, and it is one of several signs that the letter comes from a very early, Jewish-Christian setting. The social tension James describes was real in first-century Palestine and elsewhere: a small wealthy class owned much of the land, and many believers were poor laborers or tenants. Verse 6 says the rich oppress believers and drag them into court, probably over debts or wages, and verse 7 says they blaspheme the name by which believers are called, which suggests some of these rich were outsiders hostile to the faith.

If the letter was written before Paul's letters were widely known, James's argument about faith and deeds may be addressed to a common problem of religious life, the claim to believe without obeying. If it was written later, many scholars think James is answering people who had turned Paul's teaching about faith into a slogan that excused inaction. Either setting fits the text, and the question is debated.
cultural:
In the ancient world, clothing and jewelry announced rank. In Roman society a gold ring could be a mark of the equestrian order, the second tier of the aristocracy, and fine or bright clothing showed wealth. Seating in public gatherings, from theaters to banquets, was arranged by status, and patrons expected honor from their clients. James's scene of a rich man offered a good seat while a poor man is told to stand or sit on the floor reflects how every other gathering in the city worked, which is why it was so tempting.

James's readers knew the law and the Scriptures. The royal law, “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), was called by Jesus the second great commandment (Mark 12:31). The affirmation that God is one echoes the Shema, “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4), which devout Jews recited daily. Abraham was honored as the model of faith and called the friend of God (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8). Rahab's story (Joshua 2; 6) was known well enough that she became a byword for faith, hospitality, and repentance in Jewish tradition, and she appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:5) and in Hebrews 11:31.
literary: The chapter has two panels. Verses 1-13 build an argument against favoritism: a vivid scenario (2-4), rhetorical questions (5-7), an appeal to the law of love and the unity of the law (8-11), and a closing call to mercy (12-13). Verses 14-26 argue that faith without deeds is dead, again beginning with a scenario (the hungry brother or sister, 15-16), then an imagined objector (“You have faith and I have deeds”, verse 18), a reduction to absurdity (even demons believe, verse 19), and two scriptural examples, one an honored patriarch and one a foreign woman of doubtful reputation. James uses the style of the diatribe, a form of Greek moral teaching (also used by Paul in Romans) with imagined dialogue partners, pointed questions, and blunt address such as “O foolish man”. The same conclusion is stated three times (verses 17, 20, 26), and the final comparison with a body without breath makes it unforgettable.

outline.t: The rich man and the poor man in the assembly
The royal law and mercy over judgment
Answering the objector: even demons believe
Abraham and Rahab justified by what they did

doctrines.note: Saving faith is not bare agreement with true statements, which even demons have. It is trust in God that shows itself in action, as Abraham's faith “was working with his actions” and was “perfected by what he did.”
James asks whether a faith with no deeds can save. His answer (it cannot) does not teach that deeds earn salvation, but that the faith God saves by is always living and fruitful.
The law of love is the “royal law”, and the whole law is one: breaking one command makes a person a lawbreaker. James calls it “the law that gives freedom”, the law as fulfilled and taught by Jesus.
“Mercy triumphs over judgment.” Those who show no mercy will receive none, echoing Jesus' teaching (Matthew 5:7; 6:14-15). The way believers treat the poor will be weighed at the judgment.

words.note: Ergon, a work or deed. It appears twelve times in this chapter. For James, works are concrete acts of faith and mercy, such as feeding the hungry, welcoming spies, or offering Isaac. When Paul warns against works of the law as a basis for being declared right with God (Romans 3:28), he usually has in view obedience to the law's requirements, including marks such as circumcision; James has in view the fruit of faith.

Dikaioō, to justify, declare righteous, or show to be righteous. The word can refer to a verdict pronounced (as often in Paul) or to a vindication, showing someone to be what they are (as in Luke 7:35, where wisdom is vindicated by her children). Many interpreters think James uses it in this second sense, while Paul uses it for God's verdict on sinners.

Pistis, faith, trust, or belief. It appears thirteen times here. James does not reject faith; he distinguishes faith that is alive from faith that is dead. The faith he attacks is a claim (“if someone claims to have faith”, verse 14) and a creed held without trust or obedience.

Sunagōgē, assembly or synagogue. In verse 2 it names the gathering of believers, rendered “meeting” by the BSB. The word shows how naturally the earliest Jewish believers in Jesus described their worship with the vocabulary of Israel.

christ: James calls Jesus “our glorious Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 1), and this is the heart of his argument against favoritism. If believers truly hold faith in the Lord of glory, earthly glory (a gold ring, fine clothes) should not impress them. The Lord of glory himself became poor, and in the Gospels he declares the poor blessed and the kingdom theirs (Luke 6:20), which is the background to verse 5. The royal law of love is the command Jesus named as the second greatest, and the call to mercy echoes his beatitude on the merciful. Christ is also the one in whom the faith of Abraham reaches its goal: the father of believers offered his son on the altar, and the New Testament sees in the Father's giving of his own Son the fulfillment of that story (compare John 3:16; Romans 8:32).

hard.q: James says “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone,” while Paul says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. How can both be true?
hard.a: The tension is real on the surface, and Martin Luther, in his 1522 preface to the New Testament, famously ranked James below the letters he thought showed Christ most clearly. Christians have offered several reconciliations, often combining them. One focuses on the verb: Paul uses justify for God's verdict declaring a sinner righteous, while James uses it for the demonstration or vindication of that righteousness, as Abraham's faith, credited as righteousness in Genesis 15, was shown and completed decades later in Genesis 22. A second focuses on the word faith: Paul means trusting reliance on Christ that works through love (Galatians 5:6), while James attacks a faith of mere assent, the kind demons have. A third focuses on works: Paul rejects works of the law as a ground of acceptance, especially the marks of Jewish identity required of Gentiles, while James requires works of mercy as the fruit of faith. A fourth suggests James is correcting people who had misused Pauline slogans, which would mean he and Paul share the same target from opposite sides. Roman Catholic teaching, set out at the Council of Trent in 1547, reads James 2:24 as describing growth in justification through good works done by God's grace, while Protestant traditions hold that justification is a once-for-all verdict received by faith alone, with works as its necessary fruit. Across these views, Christians agree that God saves by grace and that faith which never acts is not the faith that saves.

questions: In what subtle ways does your church or community give better seats, literal or figurative, to the wealthy, the attractive, or the influential?
James uses the example of words of blessing without help for the hungry. Where are your words of faith running ahead of your deeds?
Abraham and Rahab are very different people. What does their pairing suggest about who can have living faith?
